summary:
Bahrain Climate Trend Detective is a free, interactive dashboard showing how Bahrain's land surface has changed since 2003, and whether each change is statistically real or just year-to-year noise.

The problem: Bahrain is warming fastest at night, at about 1.2 °C per decade, roughly double the daytime rate. This means hotter homes, higher cooling costs, and more heat stress, but planners lacked accessible data on where it's happening.

How it works: Users pick one of four variables (day or night land temperature, vegetation, rainfall), choose a period, adjust the strictness of the analysis, view overlays like urban growth and land reclamation, compare any cell with Bahrain's average, and upload their own data. The method uses Mann-Kendall to detect trends, Sen's slope to measure change per decade, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction to filter out chance results.

Data: NASA's MODIS (temperature, vegetation) and GPM IMERG (rainfall), processed via Google Earth Engine.

Case studies: urban growth and temperature, land reclamation, northern vegetation loss, and whether rainfall changes are genuine.

Key message: Not every change is a real trend; test before trusting.

A team of engineering students built it in 48 hours.
details:
Bahrain Climate Trend Detective. The app lets a user pick an Earth-science variable over Bahrain, see how it changed from about 2003 to 2024, and see where the change is statistically significant.

What the app will answer: Where in Bahrain is land surface getting hotter fastest? Where is vegetation gaining or being lost? Is rainfall changing? Do these hot spots match new reclamation and urban growth?

The problem​

Bahrain is getting hotter, and fastest at night. Over the last 21-22 years, night-time land temperatures have risen by 1.2 °C per decade, about twice the daytime rate. Hotter nights mean homes that never cool down, higher air-conditioning bills, and more heat stress for workers and older people. Planners need to know where this is happening and whether the change is real. Until now, that information was locked inside satellite archives.

And the product: So we built Bahrain Climate Trend Detective. It is a free, interactive web dashboard. Anyone can choose one of 5 variables  (day or night temperature, vegetation or rainfall) and see how it has changed over Bahrain since 2003. It also shows whether each change is statistically significant or just year-to-year noise.

Bahrain Climate Trend Detective is an interactive web tool that answers a simple but often overlooked question: which of Bahrain's climate changes since 2003 are real, and which are just year-to-year noise? It uses real NASA satellite observations from 2003 to 2025, covering land surface temperature and vegetation (MODIS) and rainfall (GPM IMERG), and averages each map cell into yearly values. It then applies the Mann-Kendall test to detect a consistent trend, Sen's slope to measure its size per decade, and an optional Benjamini-Hochberg correction to filter out false discoveries that arise when many cells are tested at once. Only cells that pass the test appear in full colour; the rest stay grey. Users can choose the variable, the time period and the level of statistical proof, and overlay land-reclamation and urban-growth zones to see whether hot spots follow how Bahrain's land has changed. We retrieved and processed the data with NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS, built the interactive dashboard in Looker Studio, and published the tool online with Netlify. Its main benefit is clarity: it turns large, complex satellite datasets into evidence that non-specialists can trust, helping city planners, the Bahrain Space Agency, researchers and engineers base decisions on statistically real trends rather than on single hot or wet years. The intended impact is better-informed planning for urban heat, vegetation loss and rainfall extremes. From an engineering perspective, rising surface temperatures increase heat gain in buildings and the load on air-conditioning systems, so the map shows where cooling and energy demand are likely to grow fastest. The project is creative in its "test before you trust" approach: instead of showing raw changes, it puts statistical significance at the centre of the map and lets users set the burden of proof themselves. In developing it, our team considered the different data resolutions (1 km for temperature, 250 m for vegetation and about 11 km for rainfall), cloud gaps (handled through MODIS 8-day and 16-day composites), the difference between surface and air temperature, the risk of false positives across many map cells, coastal pixels where land and sea mix, and the need for a design simple enough for non-experts to use.

The main message of our project is that not every environmental change is a real trend. We need to test the data before trusting the results. Our platform also allows anyone to upload their own data and apply the same analysis to investigate environmental changes.

None of this came ready-made. We collected 21 years of NASA satellite data through Giovanni and AppEEARS and cleaned every series year by year. We tested each series, and built our own trend calculator to run the statistics. Then we turned everything into a live dashboard and website, all within 48 hours, as a team of civil architectural & mechanical engineering students.
